nameStory: Crested Elsholtzia gets its 'crested' name from its distinctive flower spikes that rise like little crowns above the plant. The genus name Elsholtzia honors Johann Sigismund Elsholtz, a 17th-century German botanist and physician. In its native Asia, this aromatic herb goes by many flavorful names like Vietnamese balm and lemon mint, hinting at its culinary uses.
description: Crested Elsholtzia is an annual herb in the mint family that typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. Like other mints, it has square stems and opposite leaves that release a pleasant, lemony-minty fragrance when crushed. The plant produces distinctive dense, spike-like clusters of tiny white to pale pink flowers that arch gracefully at the tips, giving them their characteristic 'crested' appearance. Originally from Asia, this aromatic immigrant has found a home in parts of New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, curved flower spikes that arch at the tips like tiny shepherd's crooks, packed with small white to pale pink tubular flowers that bloom from late summer into fall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite, oval leaves with serrated edges that release a strong, pleasant lemony-mint aroma when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual herb growing 1-3 feet tall with a bushy appearance and multiple branching stems

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that are characteristic of the mint family - roll them between your fingers to feel the four distinct edges

habitat: Look for Crested Elsholtzia in disturbed soils, gardens, waste places, and along roadsides where the ground has been turned over. It prefers well-drained, fertile soils and full to partial sun. As an introduced species that's still establishing itself in New England, it's most likely to pop up in areas with human activity rather than deep wilderness.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge from seed in late spring, developing their characteristic square stems and aromatic opposite leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow bushy and tall through summer, building up their fragrant foliage but not yet flowering.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive curved flower spikes appear in late summer and persist through early fall, making this the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil for next year's generation.

funFact: This plant is so beloved in Vietnamese cuisine that it's commonly sold in Vietnamese grocery stores across America as 'kinh gioi' - the leaves add a unique lemony-mint flavor to soups and are considered essential for certain traditional dishes, making it one of the few wild New England plants you might find in the produce aisle!
confusionNotes: The curved, crested flower spikes are quite distinctive and help separate this from other mints, which typically have more upright or whorled flower clusters. The strong lemony fragrance when leaves are crushed is also a good distinguishing feature from most native mints.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the many common names confuse you - Vietnamese balm, crested late summer mint, and kinh gioi all refer to the same plant. The variety of names reflects its importance in different cultural contexts, from wild plant identification to ethnic cuisine.
compareHints: Since Crested Elsholtzia is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other mints in the Lamiaceae family. Unlike most native mints with their upright flower spikes or clustered flowers, Elsholtzia's curved, crested flower heads are unique. The timing also helps - most native mints flower earlier in summer, while this species waits until late summer to bloom.
